newsitem.title: USA: U.S. suspends military flights off East Coast.
newsitem.headline: U.S. suspends military flights off East Coast.

text.p: The U.S. Air Force on Friday suspended military flight operations in designated training areas off the East Coast after two tense incidents involving close brushes between civilian planes and F-16 fighter jets.

In addition, the Federal Aviation Administration asked controllers at its Jacksonville, Washington and New York air traffic control centers, and military controllers at the Virginia Capes station, to review procedures for handling traffic in those areas.

The action came hours after an American Eagle pilot reported that four national guard F-16 jets flew "too close" to his passenger plane off the coast of Maryland in the second such incident in three days.

On Wednesday, the operator of a Boeing 727 charter jet with about 80 passengers on board said it had a near collision with two F-16s off the coast of New Jersey. It maneuvered violently in response to electronic cockpit instrument warnings when it was approached by one of the national guard fighters.

The flight suspension order was made by Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ronald Fogelman, who said flights were being halted in "designated warning areas" normally set aside for training flights until all units had reviewed procedures with the FAA and other agencies.
The brief announcement said that the stand-down of operations included active duty, reserve and national guard aircraft.

Federal Aviation Administration spokeswoman Diane Stitaliere said that the American Eagle commercial plane, flying from Raleigh, North Carolina, to John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, reported that the military jets came too close.

The pilot told air traffic controllers in Leesburg, Virginia, he planned to file a "near mid-air collision" report of the incident, which occurred when the passenger plane was flying at about 19,000 feet (5,791 metres), she said.

At the Pentagon, however, the commander of the U.S. Air National Guard said "there was no imminent collision" and that the four fighters from the District of Columbia Air National Guard did not come dangerously close to the twin-engine plane.
"My opinion about flight off the East Coast is that it is very safe," Air Force Maj. Gen. Donald Shepperd said in response to questions from reporters, before the flight suspension was announced.

Shepperd said at the Pentagon that the four F-16s returned normally to their base at Andrews Air Force Base, Maryland, after Friday's incident, which occurred at about 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT) about 15 miles (24 km) east of the Maryland coast over the Atlantic Ocean.

Shepperd said that both incidents were under investigation and that he had no indication that any of the military pilots had done anything wrong. Civilian aviation authorities were also investigating the reports.
"All four of the F-16s had the airliner in sight, I would like to stress that," he said. "And they proceeded and landed normally at home."
He said that the American Eagle commercial plane was at an altitude of about 19,000 feet and that three of the jets flew over it, but were at least 2,000 feet (610 metres) above the commercial plane.
The fourth F-16, he said, was ahead of the American Eagle flight at an altitude of about 17,500 feet (5,334 metres) and was descending.
